passages.where: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city coming down out of heaven from God. The voice from the throne does not announce that people have gone up to God, but that God's dwelling is now with them. The end of the Bible's story is not an escape from the world but God making his home in a world made new.

Isaiah sees the LORD preparing a feast of rich food and aged wine for all peoples on his mountain. There he will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from every face. Many readers see in this chapter a key step in the Old Testament's growing hope of resurrection, and Paul quotes it when he writes that death has been swallowed up in victory.

On the night before his death, Jesus tells his frightened disciples that his Father's house has many rooms, that he is going to prepare a place for them, and that he will come back and take them to himself. The heart of the promise is not the room but the company: that you also may be where I am.

Paul, in prison and not knowing whether he will live, says that to depart and be with Christ is far better. Most Christians through history have read this as teaching that believers who die are with Christ at once, before the resurrection of the body. Paul also chooses to remain for the sake of others; longing for Christ never made him wish his work undone.

Paul answers the question of what kind of body the dead will have. Sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in weakness, raised in power; sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body. The site's note insists that a spiritual body is still a body, given life by God's Spirit, not a ghost; the risen Jesus ate and could be touched.

Paul says the whole creation waits with eager longing, subjected to futility but in hope, because it too will be set free from its bondage to decay. As the site's note puts it, Paul's hope is not that God will throw the world away and take souls to heaven, but that he will set creation itself free. Christians differ on the details.

At the very end John sees the river of life, the tree of life whose leaves heal the nations, and no more curse. God's servants will serve him and see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. The last gift of the Bible is not a place but a face: God seen without fear.

John marvels that believers are already called children of God, and admits that what they will be has not yet been made known. What he does know is this: when Christ appears, we will be like him, for we will see him as he is. The Bible is more sure of who will be there than of every detail of the place.

Hebrews says the patriarchs died in faith without receiving what was promised, confessing that they were strangers on the earth. They longed for a better country, a heavenly one. So God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

Paul reminds a church in a Roman colony that their citizenship is in heaven, and that they wait for a Savior from there. He will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body. The Christian hope runs through the body, not around it.

misread.taken: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard” is usually quoted as a verse about heaven alone: something so wonderful that no one can know anything about it until they get there.
misread.says: That is a true hope, and Paul shares it, but in its place the verse says more. Paul is speaking of God's wisdom in the cross, hidden from the rulers of this age who crucified the Lord of glory. The very next verse says, “But God has revealed it to us by the Spirit.” What no eye had seen, God has now made known in Christ. The verse is not only about the life to come; it is about what God has already shown.

whole: If you are grieving someone who has died, these words do not ask you to stop grieving, and if your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please speak to someone today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Longing for heaven is not the same as wanting to leave this life early: Paul longed to be with Christ and chose to stay for the sake of others. Many people's picture of heaven is vague: clouds, harps, souls drifting somewhere bright, an endless church service. To some it sounds dull, and to others too good to be true. People wonder whether they will know their loved ones, what happens at the moment of death, and whether any of this is more than wishful thinking.

Scripture's picture is more solid, and in some ways more surprising. The end of the story is not souls leaving the earth but God coming to dwell with his people in a new heaven and a new earth. Creation itself will be set free from decay. The dead will be raised in bodies, real bodies made imperishable, like the risen Jesus who could be touched and ate in front of his friends. Death will be swallowed up and tears wiped away. At the center is not a place but a person: they will see his face. The Christian hope does not rest on near-death reports or private visions; Paul, who had such an experience, refused to build anything on it. It rests on the claim that Jesus himself was raised, and that what happened to him will happen to those who are his.

This hope changes how life is lived now. If the body will be raised, the body matters, and so does the created world God means to set free. If the dead in Christ are with him, grief can be real and still not be hopeless. If the patriarchs could live as strangers longing for a better country, Christians can hold possessions, success and even suffering more loosely. And if the last gift is to see God's face, then the most important preparation is not speculation about the details but knowing him now. John said that everyone who has this hope purifies himself.

There is much Scripture does not say. It does not answer every question about the time between death and the resurrection, and faithful Christians read the details differently, as the section below sets out. It says enough. Jesus told his friends that he was going to prepare a place and would come back to take them to himself, so that where he is, they may be also. The feast Isaiah saw is for all peoples. The Christian hope is not an escape from this world but its healing, and its center is not what we will have but whom we will see.

differ.share: Christians confess together, with the historic creeds, that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, that the dead will be raised, and that there is a life of the world to come in which God will dwell with his people.

views.name: With the Lord at once
views.body: Most Christians hold that those who die in Christ are with him at once, aware and at rest, while they wait for the resurrection of the body. They point to Paul's longing to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), to being away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and to Jesus' promise to the man on the cross beside him (Luke 23:43).

views.name: Asleep until the resurrection
views.body: Some Christians, Seventh-day Adventists among them, read the Bible's language of sleep to mean that the dead are not conscious until the resurrection, when they will wake to the life to come. They note that the Old Testament speaks of the dead in silence, and they read Jesus' words to the man on the cross as a promise made that day and kept at the resurrection.

views.name: Prayer and purification
views.body: The Catholic and Orthodox churches pray for the dead, and Catholic teaching speaks of purgatory, a final purification of those who die in God's grace before they see him. Most Protestant churches do not pray for the dead or teach purgatory.

differ.after: All of them grieve with hope in the same risen Lord, and all of them look to the same last day. The site's notes on 2 Corinthians 5 and Luke 23 set out these readings without choosing.

sit: If the heart of heaven is seeing God's face, what in your life now is teaching you to want that?

prayer.lead: David's one request: to dwell in the house of the LORD and gaze on his beauty. Pray it as the desire underneath every other hope about heaven.

careLines.text: If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving.
If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
